description: Brute force to optimized: backtracking over every combination of matches versus a greedy prefix-sum scan that takes the earliest match and resets.

blocks.text: Given nums and target, greedily choose as many non-overlapping subarrays as possible, each summing exactly to target, maximizing the total count chosen.

blocks.title: Analogy: Cutting the Shortest Possible Ribbon Segments to Maximize Count
blocks.text: Like cutting a long ribbon into as many non-overlapping segments as possible, where each segment must have a specific target "weight". Always making the very next cut as soon as a valid segment is found (rather than waiting to see if a longer segment starting from the same point might also work) never hurts, and always leaves the maximum possible ribbon remaining for further segments.

blocks.text: Before trying every possible combination of matching subarrays to find the best non-overlapping set, notice that greedily taking the EARLIEST-ending match, then resetting completely, is always at least as good as any alternative strategy.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A subarray summing to target can be detected using a running prefix sum: if (currentPrefixSum - target) was seen at some earlier position, the subarray between that earlier position and now sums to exactly target.

Observation 2: Among all subarrays ending at any given position that could complete a match, taking the one that ends AS SOON AS POSSIBLE (the greedy choice) never leaves fewer future opportunities than taking a later-ending one would, since ending earlier only ever frees up more room afterward.

Observation 3: Once a match is taken, nothing before that cut point can ever be reused in a future (non-overlapping) match, so the prefix sum and the set of previously seen prefix sums can be reset completely, starting fresh as if a brand new array began right after the cut.

Observation 4: Repeating this greedy "detect, take, reset" cycle across the whole array in one linear pass finds the maximum possible count of non-overlapping matches.

Recognizing that greedily taking the earliest valid match is provably optimal (a classic exchange-argument style greedy, similar to interval scheduling) avoids needing to consider every possible combination of matches.

This is a greedy strategy built on prefix-sum hashing (as used for detecting target-sum subarrays generally), where the key insight is that taking the earliest match and resetting completely is always optimal.
Find every subarray summing to target directly, then use backtracking to choose the maximum non-overlapping subset among them.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, recording every (start, end) pair whose sum equals target.

Use backtracking over the recorded matches: for each match, either skip it entirely, or take it (if it doesn't overlap the most recently chosen match) and recurse, tracking the maximum count achievable.

items: Every matching subarray is found first, in a single O(n squared) pass, since the backtracking step needs the full list of candidates.
The backtracking explores both "skip this match" and "take this match" at every step, correctly considering every possible non-overlapping subset.
lastEnd tracks the most recently chosen match's ending position, ensuring only genuinely non-overlapping matches can be taken together.

blocks.text: Every possible combination of non-overlapping matches is considered via backtracking, so the correct maximum count is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) to find every match, plus O(2^k) in the worst case for the backtracking over k matches.
Space: O(k) for the recursion stack and stored matches.

Limitation: exploring every possible subset of matches via backtracking ignores that a simple greedy rule (always take the earliest-ending match, then reset) is provably optimal, avoiding the exponential search entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force explores every possible subset of matches via backtracking. Instead, greedily scan left to right with a running prefix sum and a hash set of prefix sums seen since the last cut. The moment (currentPrefixSum - target) is found in the seen set, a match completes at the earliest possible point; take it immediately, increment the count, and completely reset both the prefix sum and the seen set (since nothing before this point can ever be reused), then continue scanning from the very next position.

Maintain a hash set seen (initialized to {0}) and a running prefix sum. For each element, add it to the prefix sum, then check whether (prefix - target) is in seen. If so, increment the count and reset both prefix and seen entirely. Otherwise, add the current prefix sum to seen and continue.
Greedily scan with a running prefix sum and a hash set, taking the earliest match and resetting completely each time.

codes.python:
def max_non_overlapping(nums, target):
    seen = {0}                                                              # prefix sums seen SINCE the last cut (0 represents "no elements yet")
    prefix = 0
    count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        if prefix - target in seen:                                        # a subarray summing to target ends exactly here
            count += 1                                                     # greedily take it immediately, the earliest possible ending point
            seen = {0}                                                     # reset tracking completely; nothing before this point can be reused
            prefix = 0
        else:
            seen.add(prefix)
    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_non_overlapping([1, 1, 1, 1, 1], 2))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass, since each element is processed exactly once regardless of how many resets occur.
Space: O(n) in the worst case for the seen set (though it resets to size 1 after every successful match).

Whenever a valid target-summing subarray completes, taking it at the EARLIEST possible ending point can never be worse than waiting for a later-ending match starting from the same or an earlier position, since ending earlier only ever leaves MORE of the array available for subsequent matches, never less. This greedy exchange argument guarantees that always taking the first detected match, then resetting completely (since nothing before the cut can be reused), accumulates the true maximum count.

The reset (seen = {0}, prefix = 0) happens immediately upon a successful match, discarding all prior prefix-sum history, since none of it can ever be reused after this cut.
count is incremented exactly once per successful greedy match, directly representing the final answer.

blocks.text: The greedy strategy of "always take the earliest-ending match, then reset completely" is provably optimal here (a classic interval-scheduling-style exchange argument), turning what looks like a combinatorial optimization problem into a single linear greedy pass.

items: Trying to find the LONGEST or otherwise "best" match at each opportunity instead of the EARLIEST one, which is unnecessary and can be slower without improving correctness.
Forgetting to reset the prefix sum and seen set completely after a successful match, which would incorrectly allow a "match" to reuse elements from before the cut.
Not proving (or at least recognizing) why the greedy choice is optimal, which risks applying greedy reasoning incorrectly to a problem where it might not actually hold.

items: Explicitly justify the greedy choice ("taking the earliest match never leaves fewer opportunities than any alternative") before coding, since interviewers specifically want to see that the greedy strategy's correctness has been reasoned through, not just assumed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximum COUNT of non-overlapping subarrays/intervals matching a condition" points toward a greedy strategy: take the earliest-ending valid option found, then continue searching from just after it, discarding all prior state.

items: How would you prove the greedy strategy is optimal? Via an exchange argument: any optimal solution's first chosen match can be replaced with the earliest-ending match without decreasing the total count, since the earliest match ends at or before the optimal solution's first match, leaving at least as much room for the rest.

How would you also report the actual chosen subarrays, not just the count? Track the (start, end) indices of each greedy match as it's found, appending to a result list instead of just incrementing a counter.

What if you wanted the maximum TOTAL LENGTH covered by non-overlapping matches, not the maximum count? This changes the objective entirely, and the simple "earliest match" greedy may no longer be optimal; a DP-based approach would likely be needed instead.

Combines prefix-sum hashing (for detecting target-sum subarrays, as in Subarray Sum Equals K) with a greedy "earliest valid choice, then reset" strategy, structurally similar to classic interval scheduling's "earliest finish time" greedy rule.

blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) + O(2^k) time, O(k) space.
Optimized (greedy prefix-sum scan with reset): O(n) time, O(n) space.
